$comment: Six Boeing aircraft spanning gear codes D, 2D, 3D and 2D/2D2.
TWO DIFFERENT SOURCING METHODS LIVE IN THIS FILE.
as authoritative, from the FAA database, and DERIVE the gear centerlines
from it, because no consulted source publishes their track directly. See
The two 747s invert it. Their ACAP section 7.2 footprint figures publish the
track, both gear positions, and every spacing outright, so the geometry is
read off the figure and the outer width becomes a CROSS-CHECK rather than an
input. That is the better arrangement wherever the data allows it — it is
simply not available for the other four.
The 747s were absent until v1.6 because a single outer width cannot close a
four-bogie layout the way it closes a two-strut one: the body gear's offset
from the wing gear is a free parameter that no summary table carries. The
ACAP figures state it (10 ft 1 in, and the two models agree independently),
which is what made these entries possible without inventing geometry.
See data/SOURCES.md section 5 for what is and is not verified.

Longitudinal position = the FAA wheelbase of 51.2 ft (15 606 mm). Transverse position derived from the FAA main gear outer width of 23.0 ft (7010 mm), which the FAA data dictionary defines as the distance between outer tires: track = 7010 - 864 - 419.1 = 5727 mm, so the strut centerline sits at 2863 mm. That derived track agrees with Boeing's separately published 737 tread of 18 ft 9 in (5715 mm) to within 12 mm, which is the cross-check that supports the 864 mm (34 in) dual spacing. Longitudinal position = the FAA wheelbase of 85.8 ft (26 152 mm). Transverse position derived from the FAA main gear outer width of 36.0 ft (10 973 mm): track = 10973 - 1163 - 508 = 9302 mm, strut centerline at 4651 mm. That agrees with Boeing's published 767 tread of 30 ft 6 in (9296 mm) to within 6 mm. Tire 50x20.0R22, 32PR from Boeing 767 ACAP section 7.2.3. CORRECTED in v1.6.1: this entry previously carried a dual spacing of 1143 mm, taken as a round 45 in because no consulted source stated it. The FAARFIELD 2.1.1 aircraft library gives 45.800 in (1163.32 mm) as an explicit wheel coordinate (X +/-22.900 in), and it is the better number in the strongest available sense — because the track is DERIVED from the dual spacing, the error propagated, and 1143 was what made this aircraft's tread cross-check the worst of the four at 26 mm against 12, -13 and -10 for the others. At 1163 the residual falls to 6 mm and the outlier disappears. What moves: the OUTBOARD tire of each dual pair does not move at all, because the FAA outer width is the authoritative datum and is held; the INBOARD tire moves 20 mm inboard, and the strut centerline 10 mm. That is the derivation behaving exactly as intended — a corrected dual spacing is absorbed inside the fixed outer width rather than displacing the whole gear. ASSUMED: tandem spacing 1422 mm (56 in), declared in assumedFields; FAARFIELD gives 54.000 in for this too, but replacing it is a separate change and is not made here. Tandem spacing 1371.6 mm is no longer assumed: it is the FAARFIELD 2.1.1 aircraft library value for B767-400 ER (wheel coordinates Y ±685.8 mm), the same source this library already relies on to corroborate the 747 and A380 geometry. CORRECTED in v1.9 from the v1.2 assumption of 1422 mm (56 in), which was 50.4 mm too long. The tandem spread is symmetric about the bogie center, so it moves both axle lines and leaves the wheelbase, the track and the outer width untouched — which is exactly the property that let a wrong value sit here undetected while every other check on this aircraft passed.

mtow.basis: Boeing 747-400 ACAP D6-58326-1 Rev E (September 2023), section 2.1.1, highest Maximum Design Takeoff Weight listed for the 747-400. NOTE: the FAA Aircraft Characteristics Database lists 910 000 lb against 'Boeing 747-400'; that is the 747-400ER figure, so the manufacturer's own table is used here instead.

gears.source: Dual spacing 914 mm (36 in) read directly from the ACAP section 7.2.1 footprint figure — published, not assumed as it is on the two-strut aircraft in this library. Tire size is published as '49X17, 32 PR', a two-part Type VII designation that omits the rim diameter; the 20 in rim is ASSUMED and declared in assumedFields. Overall diameter and section width come from the published two numbers and are unaffected by that assumption.

WING gear, the outboard pair. Longitudinal position 24 067 mm = 78 ft 11.5 in, read directly from the ACAP section 7.2.1 footprint figure. Track 10 998 mm = 36 ft 1 in from the same figure, putting the strut centerline at 5499 mm — published here, not derived from the outer width as it must be for the two-strut aircraft. Cross-check: 10 998 + 1118 + 482.6 = 12 598.6 mm against the figure's own stated outer width of 41 ft 4 in (12 598.4 mm), agreeing to within 1 mm. Dual spacing 44 in and tandem spacing 58 in are the figure's TYPICAL values, and match the FAARFIELD aircraft library's B747-400 wheel coordinates exactly (X +/-22 in, Y 58 in). Tire H49X19.0-22, 32PR from the same figure.
Mirror of WLG-L about the aircraft centerline; same derivation.

BODY gear, the inboard pair — the geometry whose absence kept this aircraft out of the library until now. Longitudinal position = the wing gear's 24 067 mm plus the figure's 10 ft 1 in (3073 mm) body-gear offset. Track 3835 mm = 12 ft 7 in, strut centerline 1918 mm. Both read directly from the ACAP section 7.2.1 footprint figure. Dual and tandem spacings are that figure's TYPICAL values, which it applies to all four main bogies.
Mirror of BLG-L about the aircraft centerline; same derivation.

units.notes: Wing-plus-body gear: four main struts, sixteen main tires, eighteen in total. The body gear sits 3073 mm aft of the wing gear and 3581 mm inboard of it, so the four bogies share neither an axle line nor a track, and no single track figure describes the aircraft. The stated wheelbase is the main gear centroid, midway between wing and body gear; every bogie carries four tires, so the load centroid is the same point. NOTE: the FAA Aircraft Characteristics Database lists this aircraft's wheelbase as 87.9 ft (26 792 mm), which matches neither the wing gear, nor the body gear, nor their centroid. Boeing's figure gives 84.0 ft, the commonly published 747-400 wheelbase, and that is what is used here.

WING gear, the outboard pair. Longitudinal position 28 118 mm = 92 ft 3 in, and track 10 998 mm = 36 ft 1 in (strut centerline 5499 mm), both read directly from the ACAP section 7.2 footprint figure. Cross-check: 10 998 + 1189 + 533.4 = 12 720.4 mm against the figure's stated outer width of 41 ft 9 in (12 725.4 mm), agreeing to 5 mm — the residual is the figure's own rounding to the nearest inch. Dual spacing 46.8 in and tandem spacing 56.5 in are the figure's TYPICAL values and match the FAARFIELD library's B747-8 wheel coordinates exactly (X +/-23.4 in, Y 56.5 in). Tire 52X21.0 R22, 36PR.

BODY gear, the inboard pair. Longitudinal position = the wing gear's 28 118 mm plus the figure's 10 ft 1 in (3073 mm) body-gear offset — the same offset as the 747-400, stated independently by the two figures. Track 3835 mm = 12 ft 7 in, strut centerline 1918 mm. Cross-check on the layout as a whole: the centroid of the four bogies falls at 29 655 mm, and the FAA database's tabulated wheelbase of 97.3 ft is 29 657 mm, agreeing to 2 mm.
Mirror of BLG-L about the aircraft centerline; same derivation.

units.notes: The stretched 747, and the last one built. Same wing-plus-body architecture as the 747-400 and the same 3073 mm body-gear offset, but a longer wheelbase and a differently proportioned bogie: 46.8 in dual by 56.5 in tandem, against the -400's 44 by 58. Sixteen main tires, eighteen in total. Nothing on this aircraft is assumed — the ACAP figure publishes every spacing it needs.
